lesson.menu_desc: Ninety-six tracks, one chorus, and the courage to delete -- quantifiers and determiners with countable and uncountable nouns
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 14 -- How Much Is Too Much
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Henrique Tadeu Alves da Silva | Lesson 14 -- How Much Is Too Much
lesson.grammar_point: quantifiers and determiners with countable and uncountable nouns

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: with very few parts or sounds, often on purpose
a small piece of software that adds an effect to a sound
to do too much because you are excited and stop thinking clearly
having too many effects and extra parts, so it loses its natural feeling
to keep some space free so another thing can fit
one of several sounds or recordings placed on top of each other
to remove extra parts so only the important ones stay
the decision not to do too much, even when you can
a lot of things in one place, so it is hard to see or hear what matters

paras: A few years ago, a young producer sent a demo to a well-known mixing engineer. The song was good, but the session had ninety-six tracks. There were twelve layers of vocals in the chorus, six guitars, and a lot of plug-ins on every channel. The engineer listened once and wrote back with one sentence: there is too much here, and not enough song.

Most producers know that feeling. Modern software gives you plenty of tracks and hundreds of effects, and none of them costs anything. So it is easy to get carried away. You add a little reverb, then a few more harmonies, then another synth, because each idea sounds good alone. The problem is that every new layer takes some space, and the mix only has a little space to give. After a while there is so much clutter that the listener cannot find the voice.

The engineer did something simple. He stripped the chorus back to four tracks: one lead vocal, two harmonies and a bass line. Very few people would call the new version sparse, but it was much clearer, and the singer sounded closer. He did not use many plug-ins either. Most of the sound came from the recording itself. In his words, restraint is a skill, not a lack of ideas.

This does not mean that less is always better. Some songs need a lot of energy, and a big chorus can be exciting. The real question is not how many tracks you have, but how much each one adds. If a part adds hardly anything, it is probably overkill. A good arrangement leaves room for the voice, and for the listener.

items.situation: A colleague sends you a chorus with twelve vocal layers. Tell him, politely, what the problem is.
tips: There are too many layers in the chorus. The voice gets lost.

items.situation: Say how much time you have before the live show on Saturday.
tips: We have very little time, so we can only fix a few things.
little for time (uncountable), a few for things (countable).

items.situation: Somebody asks if the mix needs more reverb. Say no, and why.
tips: No, it has enough reverb. Any more would be overkill.
enough before the noun; any more = one step too far.

items.situation: Say how many people in your team really understand the format.
tips: Hardly anybody outside the music team knows how the format works.
hardly any / hardly anybody = almost none.

items.situation: Ask a producer a question about the session, with how much or how many.
tips: How many tracks are in the session, and how much of it do we really need?
how many + tracks; how much + it (uncountable idea).

items.situation: Describe one track of yours that you stripped back. What did you keep?
tips: I kept a few guitars and a little piano, and none of the synths.
Three quantifiers in one sentence: the decision, step by step.

listenings.text: Last month a band sent me a session for their single. It had a hundred and four tracks. I opened it and my first thought was: where is the singer? There were fourteen layers of backing vocals, a lot of synths, and so much reverb that the whole chorus sounded far away. The band had plenty of ideas, and that was the problem. So I muted everything except the drums, the bass and the lead vocal, and I added the other parts back one by one. If a part made the song better, it stayed. If it made hardly any difference, it went. In the end we kept about twenty tracks. The band was nervous at first. Nobody likes to hear that a few of their favorite ideas are not needed. But when they heard the new chorus, the singer said it was the first time she could hear her own voice. Very few changes in my job make people that happy.

I am the music director of a live singing show, and every week I have the same question: how much is too much? We have fifteen cameras, a band of nine, and a lot of lights, and the producers always want a little more. More dancers, more fire, more key changes. But a live show has only a few minutes for each song, and a singer has only a little air in her lungs. Last season, a young singer was given a huge arrangement with a choir and an orchestra on tape. In rehearsal, nobody could hear her. So we took away almost everything. We kept the piano, a few strings and her voice, and that was enough. She went to the final. I learned something that night. The audience does not count how many things are on the stage. They only remember one voice, and how much it made them feel.

extra_audio.text: The band sent a session with too many tracks. The engineer muted almost everything. He kept only a few parts: drums, bass and the lead vocal. He added the other parts back, one by one. Parts that made hardly any difference were deleted. The final chorus had enough energy and much less clutter.
